title: Spectrum scaling and isolation playbook
content:
Summary:
This is a pragmatic PRD-style playbook for a dedicated-capacity feature set we are calling 'Spectrum Scaling' — a unified approach that treats autoscaling, burst allowances, and tenant isolation as a single surface. The goal is to give customers predictable throughput under normal load, safe opportunistic burst when capacity permits, and graceful, observable degradation when contention occurs.

Problem statement:
- Customers on Dedicated want: predictable committed capacity for steady-state, flexible short-term headroom for traffic spikes, and strong tenant isolation SLAs for critical workloads.
- Current problems: brittle eviction semantics, opaque burst accounting, poor fairness during correlated spikes, and lack of simple operator controls to trade cost vs SLO.

Goals (measurable):
- Provide per-tenant committed capacity (unchanged).
- Enable controlled burst fabric that can expand effective capacity by up to X% for short windows (configurable per-plan).
- Ensure SLO preservation: committed-lane requests maintain 99.9% P95 latency; burst-lane requests have documented lower SLOs.
- Observability: per-tenant token/credit usage, burst debt ledger, eviction reasons, and end-to-end request traces within Console.

Non-goals:
- This doc does not propose a new billing model (billing changes TBD in a follow-up).
- We will not rewrite the serving runtime today; we rely on existing admission points and scheduler hooks.

Architecture overview:
- Lanes: each tenant supplies a profile that maps traffic to "lanes": committed, elastic-burst, opportunistic. Lanes carry SLO tags and priority weights.
- Credit ledger: tenants accrue/burn burst credits. Credits are seeded by reservation plan or purchased as bursts. Credits decay/expire to prevent perpetual debt.
- Admission controller: central gate that uses runtime signals (queue depth, latency headroom, GPU util) + credit balance to admit into different lanes.
- Isolation fences: when a tenant’s behavior crosses thresholds (noisy neighbor), they are moved into a soft-quarantine lane with stricter CPU/GPU caps and reduced burst eligibility.
- Fallbacks: automatic fallback routes to lower-cost model variants or lower-fidelity quantized variants with documented latency/quality tradeoffs.

Key behaviors and policies:
1) Elastic burst windowing:
   - Bursts are allowed in short windows (default 60s). Each admission consumes window credits proportional to tokens and nominal GPU seconds.
   - Rolling-window enforcement prevents exploitative bursts.
2) Graceful preemption and handoff:
   - When capacity is reclaimed, active burst requests are signalled to degrade path (switch to smaller batch, lower context, or sampled-kv-cache) rather than immediate termination.
3) Soft quarantine:
   - Trigger: sustained P50 latency > 2x tenant SLO for 60s, or sustained 90% GPU saturation attributed to tenant for 30s.
   - Action: move tenant to isolation lane for 5–30 minutes, reduce burst eligibility, enable telemetry hooks to notify customer and SE.
4) Tenant affinity and topology-aware packing:
   - Prefer co-locating steady tenants that have complementary peak times; schedule opportunistic work on nodes with slack while keeping affinity constraints for dedicated tenants.

Config surface (suggested API):
- tenant_capacity: {committed_rps, committed_concurrency}
- burst_policy: {max_burst_multiplier, window_seconds, credit_rate}
- isolation_thresholds: {latency_multiplier, gpu_share_pct, sustained_seconds}
- fallback_policies: [ {trigger, fallback_model_id, max_tokens, expected_quality_delta} ]
(We will translate this into concrete Console UI fields and API shapes in a follow-up doc.)

Example tenant story:
- Acme Apps has committed 1000 RPS. During a product launch they spike to 5000 RPS for 90s.
  - With Spectrum Scaling configured (max_burst_multiplier: 5, window_seconds: 120), 4000 extra RPS is admitted into the elastic lane and charged against Acme’s burst credits.
  - If underlying capacity drops suddenly, elastic lane requests are progressively degraded (lower model fidelity) before committed-lane requests are impacted.
  - If Acme’s traffic persists beyond burst credits and threshold windows, they receive a Quarantine notification and their burst eligibility is curtailed.

Observability and telemetry:
- New Console panels: per-tenant burst credit ledger, lane-level latency percentiles, eviction/reason timeline, node-level opportunistic utilization heatmap.
- Alerts: tenant-burst-debt-high, tenant-noisy-neighbor-detected, lane-saturation-warning.
- Audit logs: every admission decision (time, lane, decision-reason, credit-change).

Operator runbook (initial):
- Normal ops: monitor lane-saturation dashboards; adjust global default max_burst_multiplier if sustained capacity is under-provisioned.
- Noisy neighbor: when quarantine triggers, notify tenant, escalate to SE if SLA tier is enterprise. Consider temporary hard-eviction only after repeated behavior.
- Incident: if global node saturation > 95%, enable auto-backfill to spare cloud region or start emergency prewarm pool.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: burst usage can cause oscillation if not smoothed. Mitigation: use longer cooldowns and rolling-window consumption, conservative default multipliers.
- Risk: customer confusion about which requests are charged as bursts. Mitigation: clear Console labels, sample request traces with lane tag, and customer-visible burst ledger.
- Risk: subtle fairness regressions across tenants. Mitigation: incorporate fairness scoring in the admission controller and run simulated workload tests.

Rollout plan (phased):
- Phase 0 (internal): implement admission controller hooks and credit ledger, enable on staging with synthetic noisy tenants. 6 weeks.
- Phase 1 (pilot): small set of enterprise customers opt-in; gather data on credit burn patterns and false positive quarantines. 4–6 weeks.
- Phase 2 (opt-in GA): available in Console for all Dedicated customers under a feature flag. 8–12 weeks.
- Phase 3 (GA + defaults): enable conservative defaults for new Dedicated accounts; continue to iterate on UI/metrics.

Open questions for follow-up:
- Billing integration model for burst credits vs metered overage.
- Exact decay/expiration parameters for credit ledger and how refunds should work.
- UX for customers to request temporary increases (one-click surge buy) and how to sign the associated SLA.

Next steps / action items:
- Product to finalize API shapes, Contract to review enterprise billing impact (owner: Rina).
- Infra to prototype admission controller and credit ledger (owner: Miguel).
- Applied ML to evaluate model-fidelity fallback impact on perceived quality for the top 10 customer prompts (owner: Evan).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally operational and prescriptive rather than a deep speculative design. The intent is to create a playbook we can execute against in the next 3 months and to capture edge cases we consistently see in Dedicated ops.

References and links:
- Related pilot notes: Confluence: dedicated-surge-pilot (linked above)
- Sim tests: github.com/redwood-inference/load-sims (see experiment/spectrum-2024)

Appendix: quick glossary
- Committed lane: tenant traffic guaranteed by reservation.
- Elastic-burst lane: short-lived headroom above committed capacity, tied to credits.
- Opportunistic lane: lowest priority work that can be scheduled on leftover capacity; preemptible.
- Quarantine: temporary isolation state used to protect cluster SLOs.

-- Aisha
